segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ dṛḍhīkaraṇāya kṛṣṇācāryacaraṇaiś caryāntaram abhihitam —
segments.translation: To make that same meaning firm, the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} has spoken another song of [conduct]{carya}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces song 19 as another song of [conduct]{carya} by [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, spoken to make firm 'that same meaning' already set out (cp.19.m1). The Tibetan translation instead has him 'teaching the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don bstan par byed pa), where bstan, 'teach', may be a slip for brtan, 'make firm'.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don bstan par byed pa'i nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyis, 'by Kṛṣṇacārin, who teaches the meaning of reality', where the Sanskrit has 'to make that same meaning firm'. De kho na nyid may only render tam eva, 'that very' (the Tibetan uses de nyid and de kho na nyid for sā eva in cp.19.m2, m3 and m5), and bstan, 'teach', may be a slip for brtan, 'make firm'. The Tibetan also makes the phrase describe Kāṇha rather than state his purpose. I translate the Sanskrit.
caryāntaram, 'another caryā': rendered 'another song of conduct', keeping the glossary's 'conduct' while making clear that a song is meant; the Tibetan has glu dbyangs gzhan, 'another song'.

segments.translit: bhavanirvāṇe ityādi | bhavanirvāṇaṃ manapavanādivikalpaṃ pūrvoktaṃ krameṇa pariśodhyaṃ taṃ paṭahādibhāṇḍam utprekṣya mahāsukhasaṅgaṃ gṛhītvā | ḍombīti saiva śukranāḍikā 'pariśuddhāvadhūtikā tasyā[ḥ] vāhavabhaṅgārthaṃ yadā kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ pracalitāḥ | tadā jayajayadhvanipuṣpavṛṣṭidundubhiśabdādikam ākāśe nimittaṃ prabhūtam iti |
segments.translation: '[Existence and nirvāṇa]{bhava-nirvana}' and so on. [Existence and nirvāṇa]{bhava-nirvana} are the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of [mind and wind]{mana-pavana} and the rest, spoken of before, which is to be purified in sequence. Imagining it as the instruments beginning with the [paṭaha]{pataha}, and taking [great bliss]{mahasukha} as [companion]{companion} — '[Ḍombī]{dombi}': she is none other than the [channel of semen]{sukranadika}, the unpurified [avadhūtikā]{avadhuti} — when the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} set out to break her flow, then omens arose in the sky: the [sound]{dhvani} of 'victory, victory', a rain of flowers, the sound of the [kettledrum]{dundubhi} and the rest.
segments.note: Munidatta reads [existence and nirvāṇa]{bhava-nirvana} as the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of mind, wind and the rest, to be purified in sequence and imagined as the drums; [Ḍombī]{dombi} as the [channel of semen]{sukranadika}, the unpurified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, whose flow [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} sets out to break; the refrain's victory cries and [kettledrum]{dundubhi} as omens in the sky (cp.19.m2). The Tibetan makes the thought 'nonconceptual'.

equations.en: the conceptual thought of mind, wind and the rest, spoken of before, to be purified in sequence (imagined as the instruments beginning with the paṭaha)
the channel of semen, the unpurified avadhūtikā

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit has manapavanādivikalpa, 'the conceptual thought of mind, wind and the rest', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has yid dang rlung la sogs pa rnam par mi rtog pa, 'the nonconceptual state of mind, wind and the rest': a negative the Sanskrit lacks. It also joins 'spoken of before' to the sequence (sngon du gsungs pa'i rim pas yongs su sbyangs pa, 'purified by the sequence taught before'), so that the purifying is done and not still to be done (pariśodhya), and it has 'khor ba, 'saṃsāra', for bhava. I translate the Sanskrit.

paṭahādibhāṇḍa: 'the instruments beginning with the paṭaha' (bhāṇḍa can mean musical instruments, which suits the drums of the song). The Tibetan takes bhāṇḍa as snod, 'vessel' (rnga pa Ta ha la sogs pa snod du nye bar bltas te).

vāhavabhaṅgārtham, 'to break her flow': vāhava is not a regular word; I take it as vāha, 'flow, carrying'. The Tibetan 'dzag pa gzhom pa'i phyir, 'to destroy her leaking', supports that sense. The phrase stands where the refrain (2b) has bibāhe, 'for the marriage', apparently a play on vi-vāha; compare cp.19.m3.
mahāsukhasaṅgaṃ gṛhītvā: 'taking great bliss as companion' follows the Tibetan bde ba chen po'i grogs bzung nas; saṅga can also mean contact or union ('taking up union with great bliss').

The gerunds utprekṣya and gṛhītvā have no subject until yadā kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ pracalitāḥ, with the gloss on Ḍombī set in between. I take Kṛṣṇācārya as the subject of all three and mark the interruption with dashes. The honorific plural kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ is rendered 'the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya'.
nimittaṃ prabhūtam: I take prabhūta as 'arose, came forth' (the Tibetan has rab tu byung ba); it can also mean 'abundant' ('omens in abundance').

This segment also covers the refrain (couplet 2), which has no comment of its own: the cries of victory and the kettledrum of 2a become omens in the sky, and Kāṇha's setting out in 2b becomes setting out to break Ḍombī's flow. The Tibetan renders the cry as an optative, rgyal bar gyur cig, 'may he be victorious!', treated as a lemma (ces pa ni); its line 2a places the great drum in the sky (mkha' la rnga chen sgra), as Munidatta's ākāśe does.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena ḍombīvivāhaphalam āha —
ḍombītyādi | saiva ḍombī vāyurūpā tasya gamanadvārasya vivāham iti | bhaṅgaṃ kṛtvā jayam iti | utpādabhaṅgādidoṣā nāśitāḥ | ata eva jautakenākleśenānuttaradharmasākṣātkṛtaṃ mayā kṛṣṇācāryeṇeti |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the fruit of the [marriage]{vivaha} with [Ḍombī]{dombi}: '[Ḍombī]{dombi}' and so on. That same [Ḍombī]{dombi} has the form of [wind]{vayu}; the '[marriage]{vivaha}' is that of the door by which it goes. Having made the break, victory. The faults of [arising and perishing]{utpada-bhanga} and the rest have been destroyed. For that very reason, by the [dowry]{yautuka}, without [affliction]{klesa}, the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [dharma]{dharma} has been directly realized by me, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet the fruit of the [marriage]{vivaha}. [Ḍombī]{dombi} is [wind]{vayu}, and the 'marriage' concerns the door by which it goes (the Tibetan: its going is to be destroyed). With the break comes victory: the faults of [arising and perishing]{utpada-bhanga} are destroyed, and by the [dowry]{yautuka} [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has directly realized the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [dharma]{dharma}, without [affliction]{klesa} (cp.19.m3).

equations.en: the 'marriage' of the door by which the wind goes; apparently taken as vi-vāha, the stopping of its flow

flags.note: vivāha: once Ḍombī is called wind, 'the marriage is that of the door of its going' (tasya gamanadvārasya vivāham) seems to take vivāha as vi-vāha, the stopping of the flow, as vāhavabhaṅga does in cp.19.m2. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no word for marriage here: de'i 'gro ba'i sgo nas 'gro ba gzhom par bya'o, 'through the door of its going, its going is to be destroyed'. I keep 'marriage' and leave the play to the note.

bhaṅgaṃ kṛtvā jayam iti, 'having made the break, victory', quotes no word of the song. It seems to gloss ahāriu jāma (3a), with utpādabhaṅgādidoṣā nāśitāḥ taking up jāma, 'birth' (the Tibetan marks skye ba'i, 'of birth', as the lemma there). If so, Munidatta took ahāriu as 'defeated, conquered' (compare Bengali hār-, 'lose, be defeated'), not 'ate up' as in the draft. The Tibetan line instead reads āhāra, 'food' (kha zas sbyar, 'prepared the food'), and the Tibetan comment has no 'victory'.

akleśena: 'without affliction' follows the glossary and the Tibetan nyon mongs pa med pa; as a Sanskrit adverb it usually means 'without trouble, effortlessly'. The Tibetan attaches it to the dharma ('the unsurpassed dharmatā free of afflictions') rather than to the realizing.

The Tibetan has de kho na nyid Dom+bi nI ('Ḍombī, reality', or simply 'that very Ḍombī') for saiva ḍombī; chos nyid, 'dharmatā', for dharma; and zhal mthong ston mo, 'the feast of seeing the face', for jautaka, 'dowry'.
tasya is masculine or neuter, so 'the door by which it goes' refers to the wind (vāyu), not to Ḍombī (feminine). jautaka is Munidatta's form of yautuka, 'dowry'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena yoginīprabhāvam āha | ahaṇisītyādi —
etayā jñānamudrayā saha yasya yogīndrasyāharniśaṃ suratābhiṣvaṅgo bhavati tasya yogīndrasya yoginījāleneti | tasya jñānaraśminā | raeṇītyādi | kleśāndhakāraṃ palāyate |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
ātmany eva layaṃ gate bhagavati prāṇādhipe svāmini
śvāsocchvāsagaṇe gate praśamite jīvānile yantrite |
yo jyotiḥprasaraḥ prabhāsvarataro yogīśvarāṇām asau
svāṅgād eva vinirgato hatatamāḥ trailokyam ākrāmati ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the power of the [yoginī]{yogini}: 'Day and night' and so on. For the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} who has [attachment]{abhisvanga} day and night to [lovemaking]{surata} with this [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}, 'by the [net of yoginīs]{yoginijala}' of that [lord of yogis]{yogindra} means: by his rays of knowledge. '[Night]{rajani}' and so on: the darkness of the [afflictions]{klesa} flees. And so the [scripture]{agama}:
When the blessed lord of breath, the master, has gone to dissolution in the self alone,
when the host of in-breaths and out-breaths has gone and is stilled, and the life [wind]{vayu} is reined in,
the stream of light of the [lords of yogis]{yogindra}, exceedingly radiant,
comes forth from their own body, slays the darkness and overruns the [three worlds]{trailokya}.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet the [yoginī]{yogini}'s power. The [lord of yogis]{yogindra} is attached day and night to [lovemaking]{surata} with 'this [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}'; the [net of yoginīs]{yoginijala} is his rays of knowledge; the night's passing is the darkness of the afflictions fleeing. A scriptural verse on light streaming from yogis' bodies follows (cp.19.m4). The Tibetan has 'ocean of knowledge' for jñānamudrā.

equations.en: the rays of knowledge (jñānaraśmi) of the lord of yogis
the darkness of the afflictions, which flees

citations.quoted: ātmany eva layaṃ gate bhagavati prāṇādhipe svāmini … svāṅgād eva vinirgato hatatamāḥ trailokyam ākrāmati

flags.note: For etayā jñānamudrayā saha, 'with this jñānamudrā', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'dis ye shes kyi rgya mtshor lhan cig, 'by this, together with the ocean of knowledge': rgya mtsho, 'ocean', where phyag rgya, 'seal', is expected, whether a slip in the Tibetan or a reading jñānasamudra. The Tibetan also renders suratābhiṣvaṅga as shin tu dga' ba dang mngon par 'grogs pa, 'great delight and close association'.

In the verse the Tibetan has srog gi me, 'fire of life', for jīvānile, 'the life wind', as if reading anala, 'fire', for anila, 'wind'; 'od zer rab brgyad, 'rays ... eight', probably for brgyas, 'spread' (prasara); and it sets the end of the last line, 'overruns the three worlds', outside the verse as a gloss ('jig rten gsum kun du gnon pa'o). yantrite, 'reined in', has no clear equivalent, and bdag nyid thim gyur reads 'the self dissolved' rather than 'dissolved in the self'.
prabhāsvarataraḥ is a comparative adjective, 'more (or exceedingly) radiant'; I have not tagged it as the technical noun 'clear light' (prabhasvara), which it cannot render here.

yasya ... tasya yogīndrasya yoginījāleneti: I read the relative clause as defining the lord of yogis, and iti as closing the lemma 'by the net of yoginīs', which tasya jñānaraśminā, 'by his rays of knowledge', explains. Munidatta's lemma ahaṇisī corresponds to the song's ahiṇisi.

bhagavati prāṇādhipe svāmini, 'the blessed lord of breath, the master': the verse does not say who this is (the mind, the self, a deity), and I translate without deciding. The Tibetan construes it as 'the Blessed One is the lord of life' (bcom ldan 'das ni srog gi bdag po).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena yoginīprasādād yogīndrasya caryām āhuḥ —
ḍombītyādi | ḍombī saiva prakṛtiprabhāsvarapariśuddhāvadhūtikā jñānamudrā | tasyāḥ suratābhiṣvaṅge ye ye yogino ratāḥ te te tāṃ jñānamudrāṃ mahāsukhānandādhāratvāt kṣaṇam api na parityajantīti |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
sarvābhāvaṃ gatavati manasyandītyādi || 19 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [conduct]{carya} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} that comes from the [grace]{prasada} of the [yoginī]{yogini}: '[Ḍombī]{dombi}' and so on. [Ḍombī]{dombi} is none other than the [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}: the [avadhūtikā]{avadhuti}, [clear light]{prabhasvara} by nature and purified. Whichever [yogis]{yogi} delight in [attachment]{abhisvanga} to [lovemaking]{surata} with her, each of them never gives up that [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra} even for a moment, because she is the support of the [joy]{ananda} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. And so the venerable [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'When the mind has gone to the nonbeing of all…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet the [conduct]{carya} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, through the [yoginī]{yogini}'s [grace]{prasada}. [Ḍombī]{dombi} is the [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}, the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, [clear light]{prabhasvara} by nature and purified; whichever yogis delight in [lovemaking]{surata} with her never give her up for a moment, since she is the support of the joy of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. He then cites [Saraha]{p-saraha} (cp.19.m5).

equations.en: the jñānamudrā: the avadhūtikā, clear light by nature and purified

citations.work: Saraha, as Munidatta names him; the work is not named and the verse is not identified

flags.note: ye ye yogino ratāḥ ... te te, 'whichever yogis delight ... each of them', and the Tibetan line's gang gang dga', 'whoever delights', suggest a repeated relative (jo jo) in 5a, where Shastri prints jo joi and the draft has 'The yogi who'. The Tibetan line also opens with kye'i, 'O', addressing Ḍombī.

manasyandī in the Saraha quotation is unclear. I read manasi, 'the mind' (a locative absolute with gatavati), and leave andī, apparently the start of a word where the citation breaks off, untranslated. Alternatively manaḥsyandī, 'mind-flowing'. The Tibetan kun du dngos med gyur ldan 'bab, 'having become wholly without entity, ... flows', supports syand-, 'flow', renders the -vat of gatavati by ldan, and has no word for mind.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang bzhin yongs su dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI pa'i ye shes kyi phyag rgya, 'the jñānamudrā of the naturally purified avadhūtī': it lacks prabhāsvara, 'clear light', and makes the jñānamudrā the avadhūtī's rather than the avadhūtī herself. For ādhāra, 'support', it has 'dzin pa, 'holding'.
Shastri prints yoginoratāḥ as one word; read yogino ratāḥ. yoginīprasādāt is taken with caryām ('the conduct that comes from the yoginī's grace'), as the Tibetan rnal 'byor ma'i drin las also allows.

proposals.definition: Grace or favour (Sanskrit prasāda; Tibetan drin): the kindness of a teacher or deity through which realization comes. Munidatta often speaks of what is gained by the guru's grace; in song 19 he introduces the last couplet as the conduct of the lord of yogis that comes from the yoginī's grace (cp.19.m5).
proposals.rationale: Grace, the guru's or the yoginī's, recurs throughout Munidatta's comments (by the guru's grace, by the true guru's grace) but has no entry; one rendering keeps it steady across songs.

questions: Names and keep-source terms in Munidatta's Sanskrit: I tagged his own forms, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} and [avadhūtikā]{avadhuti}, rather than the approved 'Kāṇha' and 'avadhūtī' (the notes use the approved forms). Should the commentary translation use the approved forms instead?

3a ahāriu: Munidatta's 'having made the break, victory' (cp.19.m3) may show him taking ahāriu as 'defeated, conquered' rather than 'ate up'; the Tibetan line has 'food' (kha zas). Should the draft's 'I have eaten up birth' carry a flag or note on this?

5a jo joi: Munidatta's 'whichever yogis ... each of them' (cp.19.m5) and the Tibetan line's gang gang, 'whoever', point to a repeated relative 'whoever'. Keep the draft's singular 'The yogi who', or flag the line?

vivāha: in cp.19.m2 and cp.19.m3 Munidatta seems to play on vi-vāha, the stopping of flow (the Tibetan has 'to destroy her leaking' and 'its going is to be destroyed'). I kept 'marriage' in the translations and put the flow in the notes; should the play be spelled out in a note on 2b or 3a?
The Saraha quotation in cp.19.m5 breaks off at manasyandī, which I could not construe with confidence, so I left andī untranslated. If you know the verse, its reading would settle this.

The cp.19.m2 note covers couplets 1 and 2 together, anchored at cp.19.1, because Munidatta gives the refrain no comment of its own. Should the part on the refrain be split into a separate note on cp.19.2?
